title: A blessing before the battle
hookLine: the Gita is over, Arjuna has picked up his bow, and Yudhishthira takes off his armor and walks toward the enemy.
carry: ashirvad: honor your elders, even across the field

cards: The teaching ends. Arjuna tells Krishna his confusion is gone and he will do as Krishna says. He picks up his bow.
Both armies roar. And then, before a single arrow flies, Yudhishthira does something strange. He takes off his armor.
He lays down his weapons. He climbs out of his chariot and walks, on foot, straight toward the enemy lines. His brothers run after him, asking where he's going.
The other army starts to murmur that he's come to surrender. Session six of six: what the Gita leads into.

teach.h: HE BOWS AND ASKS A BLESSING
teach.b: Yudhishthira walks to Bhishma, bows to him, and asks his permission to fight him, and his blessing. Bhishma is moved.

In Ganguli's telling, he says that if Yudhishthira had not come to him like this, he would have cursed him with defeat. Instead he blesses him: fight, and win. Then he says something painfully honest about himself.
A person is a slave to wealth, but wealth is no one's slave.

teach.h: BHISHMA: I'M BOUND BY THEIR WEALTH
teach.b: I am bound to the Kauravas by their wealth. Ask me for anything except to fight on your side. So Yudhishthira asks a harder question.
How can you be beaten? No one can defeat me now, Bhishma tells him, and the time of my death has not yet come.
Ask me again another time. Yudhishthira goes on to his teachers, Drona and Kripa, and to his uncle Shalya, and does the same with each.
And when he calls out for anyone who would choose his side, one of Dhritarashtra's own sons, Yuyutsu, crosses over.

Here is something Hindu families still live by: ashirvad, the blessing of elders. Before a wedding, an exam or a journey, you bow to your elders, often touching their feet, and ask for their blessing.
Being on opposite sides doesn't cancel the bond. Yudhishthira is about to fight these men, and he won't begin without honoring them. And they bless him, even Bhishma, who leads the other army.
Many teachers read it this way: respect isn't the same as agreement, and it doesn't wait until you agree.

how: In the Mahabharata, the Gita is followed directly by Yudhishthira's unarmed walk to Bhishma, Drona, Kripa and Shalya to ask their blessing; Hindus still bow to elders, often touching their feet, to ask ashirvad before anything big.

o: the epic's book of Bhishma, where the Gita gives way to battle
the armor Yudhishthira takes off to walk across the field
the blessing the grandsire gives before the fighting starts

games.q: who did what before the battle? tap the pairs.
p: an elder's blessing, asked with a bow
takes off his armor and walks over
bound to the Kauravas by wealth

s: Yudhishthira walked to the Kaurava lines to surrender
he went unarmed to ask Bhishma and his teachers for permission and blessing.
and said that if he hadn't come, he would have cursed him.
Bhishma told Yudhishthira at once how he could be beaten
he said the time of his death had not yet come: ask again another time.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. the Gita is over and both armies are roaring. you're about to fight your own grandfather. what do you do first?
o: take off your armor and walk over to ask his blessing.
send a messenger with one last peace offer.
games.why: he walks unarmed to Bhishma and asks permission and a blessing. Bhishma gives it: honoring an elder doesn't stop at the battle line.

practice: Many Hindus touch an elder's feet, or simply fold their hands, before something big. Think of an elder you're at odds with, a little or a lot. Breathing in, see their face.

Breathing out, find one thing in them you honestly respect, and silently ask their blessing anyway, the way Yudhishthira did. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If you don't, just let the respect stay.

wordCard.voice: Bhishma Parva. The book of the grandsire who blesses his opponent, confesses what binds him, and says: ask me again.

orig.note: ashirvad, blessing: what Yudhishthira crosses the field to ask, and what Hindus ask of elders before anything big.

carryVoice: Your line: ashirvad: honor your elders, even across the field. A blessing given to the man who would fight him. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 18.73, Arjuna: my confusion is gone; I will do as you say
